name: Google Supremacy Overhype
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Ten Thousand Years, Give or Take: The Sycamore Supremacy Dispute
lesson.summary: Google's 2019 announcement that its Sycamore processor achieved quantum supremacy by beating classical supercomputers on a specific task was immediately contested by IBM and later undermined further by classical algorithm improvements, making it a textbook case of a real result oversold in translation.
lesson.body:
In October 2019, Google published a paper in the journal Nature claiming that its 53-qubit Sycamore processor had achieved quantum supremacy, completing a specific random circuit sampling task in about 200 seconds that Google's team estimated would take the world's most powerful classical supercomputer at the time, IBM's Summit, roughly ten thousand years to complete. The headline framing was dramatic and largely accurate to the paper's own claims: a quantum computer had, for the first time, solved a well-defined computational task faster than any classical machine could plausibly manage.

IBM disputed the comparison almost immediately, and the dispute is worth understanding in detail because it illustrates exactly how a real result gets amplified past what it actually shows. IBM researchers argued that Google's ten-thousand-year estimate assumed a classical simulation strategy that did not make efficient use of available disk storage, and that a better-optimized classical approach, still running on Summit, could complete the same task in roughly two and a half days rather than ten thousand years. That is an enormous difference, from millennia to about sixty hours, and it came directly from IBM's own domain experts rather than from outside critics.

Even setting aside the IBM rebuttal, the deeper problem with the supremacy claim, one that Google's own paper was reasonably careful about but that got lost in public coverage, is that the specific task Sycamore solved, random circuit sampling, was chosen precisely because it is hard for classical computers and has no known practical application. It does not simulate a useful molecule, optimize a real supply chain, or break real encryption. It was, by design, a benchmark constructed to favor quantum hardware, comparable to designing a race specifically to showcase a car's one strongest capability rather than testing overall usefulness. Winning that specific race is a genuine scientific achievement, worth publishing in Nature, but it is a narrower claim than useful quantum computer beats classical computer, which is how much of the press coverage described it.

The story continued to shift in later years as classical algorithms kept improving. Researchers, including teams connected to IBM and other groups over the following years, published further classical simulation methods that narrowed the claimed gap even beyond IBM's initial two-and-a-half-day estimate, in some analyses down to a matter of hours on well-optimized classical hardware. This is a recurring feature of supremacy-style claims across computer science generally: a task declared classically intractable at one point in time can become tractable later, not because the quantum hardware got worse, but because classical algorithms and hardware kept improving too, something the original ten-thousand-year comparison did not fully anticipate.

Fitting this into the broader catalog of broken promises, the Sycamore episode is less a case of outright false claims and more a case of a genuine, narrow, technically accurate result being carried by press coverage and public narrative into a much broader and less accurate claim: that quantum computers had definitively and permanently surpassed classical ones. That broader claim was never quite true in 2019, and the years of walkback and classical catch-up that followed are a direct, well-documented instance of the pattern this unit has been tracking since Feynman's original 1981 proposal.
